newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia media laws seen absurd - Howard.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia media laws seen absurd - Howard.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Friday that Australia's media ownership rules were absurd and that the government would determine any changes on grounds of national interest.
"I hope that we will make a conscientious national-interest decision," Howard said on Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.

"You can find just about every player in the media, including Rupert Murdoch, including my predecessor as prime minister, who at various stages have criticised the absurdity of having cross media prohibition in an age of what is called convergence between the various arms of the media," he said.
The conservative Liberal-National government is currently reviewing cross-media ownership laws, which it has described as antiquated and inflexible.
Under current cross-media regulations, media proprietors are not allowed to have large shareholdings in both broadcast and print media in the same market.
Howard also said a high degree of foreign ownership was good for the Australian economy.
"There's a sensitivity in this country about foreign ownership," Howard said.

"I've never been particularly paranoid about foreign ownership because -- if you have any understanding of the way the Australian economy operates -- a fairly high, well not high level, but perhaps a high degree of foreign ownership is indispensible if we want to maintain the sort of activities and the sort of standards of living we have," he said.
Communications Minister Richard Alston's said last June he was not predisposed to allowing increased foreign investment in Australia's media.
Foreigners are currently limited to owning 25 percent in Australian newspapers and 15 percent in television companies.
Canadian media mogul Conrad Black, who wanted to boost his 25 percent stake in publisher John Fairfax Holdings Ltd, decided in December to sell it instead to New Zealand's Brierley Investments Ltd.
Brierly took 20 percentage points of Black's holding and wants to progressively raise the stake to 25 percent.
